tldr: This research dramatically boosts the prediction and control performance of agile drones by synchronizing and coupling a world model that predicts unknown external environment motion in latent space with a differentiable simulator that computes the robot's physical motion with high precision.
hero_caption: Overall architecture of DiffDreamer. A learned latent world model (RSSM) handles future predictions of the external environment (such as dynamic gates), while a differentiable simulator handles the drone's own rigid-body physics and the propagation of analytical gradients. The policy takes states from both as inputs and outputs high-frequency collective thrust and body rate commands.
overview:
In tasks like tracking a moving target or drone racing through dynamic gates, an agent must anticipate how the other party will move next while steering the quadrotor with millisecond-level precision right at the physical limits. World-model-based reinforcement learning (such as Dreamer) is a promising approach for this challenge because it learns by imagining the world in latent space. However, forcing a single neural network to capture both the uncertain behavior of the external environment and the drone's own high-frequency rigid-body dynamics easily causes modeling errors (model bias), degrading control precision. On the other hand, differentiable reinforcement learning (DiffRL), which optimizes policies efficiently through the derivatives of a physics engine, excels at smooth robot motion control. Yet, it struggles with partial observability, unknown motion of external objects, and non-differentiable discrete events like gate crossings.

To address this, the authors developed "DiffDreamer," which combines the strengths of both paradigms. The intuition is very natural: when catching a flying ball, a human imagines the ball's trajectory in their mind while moving their muscles using an internal motor model of their own body. DiffDreamer translates this concept into a control architecture. External temporal evolution is imagined (rolled out) using an RSSM-based world model, while the robot's physical state is propagated concurrently in a differentiable simulator. Furthermore, they introduced a "dual-pathway" design where non-differentiable task rewards are optimized via a critic and smooth motion rewards are optimized via analytical gradients from the simulator.

Experiments evaluated the method on two ultra-demanding tasks: tracking an aggressively fleeing target and racing through moving gates. DiffDreamer demonstrated overwhelming performance in both training convergence speed and control accuracy compared to traditional RL, differentiable RL, and classical MPC-based methods. It also achieved zero-shot real-world flight deployment.
contributions: Proposed a dual-pathway optimization framework that time-synchronizes and concurrently rolls out a latent world model for external temporal prediction and a differentiable simulator for robot physical motion.

Developed a reward decomposition mechanism that optimizes non-differentiable task achievement rewards via a critic and smooth motion rewards directly via analytical gradients from the differentiable simulator.
Demonstrated control and prediction performance that significantly outperforms existing RL, differentiable RL, and classical MPC methods on aggressive target tracking and dynamic-gate racing tasks.
Showed that by incorporating an identified physical model, high-frequency control policies trained in simulation can be directly transferred zero-shot to a real quadrotor.

sections.heading: Why Should Prediction and Physics Control Run Separately?
sections.summary: Agile drone control demands both future prediction of dynamic environments and high-frequency physical control. This section outlines the limitations of world models and differentiable simulations, explaining DiffDreamer's motivation and contributions in tightly coupling them.
sections.details:
In tasks such as flying a quadrotor through moving gates at high speeds, an agent must anticipate the external environment's motion while controlling the platform accurately at its physical limits.

The traditional dominant approach has been a modular pipeline separating prediction, planning, and control into independent components. While highly interpretable and practical, errors easily propagate across modules to downstream controllers, and manual tuning costs run high.

On the other hand, recent world-model-based reinforcement learning methods (like Dreamer) can learn end-to-end by modeling the entire environment in latent space and "imagining" the future. However, trying to capture two fundamentally different dynamics in a single neural network—the partially observed, history-dependent motion of the external environment and the robot's own rigid-body dynamics that follow known physical laws—leads to model bias. This prevents the agent from obtaining the precise gradients needed for millisecond-level physical control.

This is where differentiable reinforcement learning (DiffRL) draws attention. It directly optimizes policies with low-variance first-order gradients using the calculus of a physics engine. While it boasts outstanding sample efficiency for smooth robot motion, it cannot handle trajectory prediction of unknown external objects or discontinuous, non-differentiable reward events like gate crossings.

DiffDreamer proposes a novel framework that structurally decouples external prediction from self-physical motion, rolling them out concurrently while keeping them time-synchronized within a single optimization step.

sections.heading: The Evolution of Modular Pipelines, Model-Based RL, and Differentiable RL
sections.summary: This section reviews traditional modular approaches in agile flight, sample-efficient model-based reinforcement learning, and differentiable reinforcement learning utilizing physics engines, summarizing their advantages and challenges.
sections.details:
### II-A Agile Flight and Modular Pipelines
In agile drone flight and autonomous racing, designing separate, pipelined modules for perception, state estimation, trajectory planning, and low-level control has been standard. For dynamic obstacles, combinations of Kalman filters, spatial-temporal trajectory optimization (such as Elastic Tracker), and MPC (Model Predictive Control) are commonly used. However, because these modules are optimized separately, prediction errors can trigger control failures—a mismatch between prediction and control that becomes prominent during high-speed flight.

### II-B Strengths and Limitations of Model-Based RL
Model-based reinforcement learning (such as MBPO and Dreamer), which learns environment dynamics to predict long-term returns, offers appealing sample efficiency from trial and error. However, in robot control where high frequency and precision are required, even minor discrepancies in the learned model can be fatal. In drones especially, external irregular motions mingle with high-speed rotational dynamics, causing control performance to plateau easily compared to physical simulation.

sections.heading: Dual-Pathway Optimization Synchronizing Imagination and Physics Simulation
sections.summary: This section describes the DiffDreamer architecture, which couples latent states capturing external temporal features with the robot's physical states and optimizes policies by backpropagating non-differentiable and differentiable rewards through separate pathways.
sections.details:
### III-A & III-B Preliminaries and Imagination via World Models
The task is formulated as a POMDP (Partially Observable Markov Decision Process). The base world model adopts the RSSM (Recurrent State-Space Model) from DreamerV3. Observations $o_t$ pass through an encoder to produce stochastic latent features $z_t$ and deterministic hidden states $h_t$. Future trajectory rollouts (imagination) take place within this combined implicit state $s_t^{\mathrm{imp}} = \{z_t, h_t\}$.

### III-C Differentiable Simulation and Equations of Motion
The robot's own state is defined as an explicit state $s_t^{\mathrm{exp}} = \{\mathbf{p}_W, \mathbf{v}_W, \mathbf{q}, \mathbf{\Omega}\}$, consisting of position, velocity, quaternion orientation, and angular velocity. The quadrotor's continuous-time rigid-body dynamics are integrated via ODEs across time steps, allowing analytical gradients $\frac{\partial s_{j}^{\mathrm{exp}}}{\partial s_{j-1}^{\mathrm{exp}}}$ to be backpropagated through time (BPTT) using the physics simulator.

### III-D DiffDreamer Integrated Design
This is the core of the paper. The policy (Actor) takes as input both the implicit state $s_t^{\mathrm{imp}}$ of the external environment predicted by the RSSM and the explicit state $s_t^{\mathrm{exp}}$ of the drone propagated by the differentiable simulator.

Feeding the same action $a_t$ into both models to advance one step at a time keeps latent external prediction and explicit physical prediction completely time-synchronized. A stop-gradient operator $\mathrm{sg}(\cdot)$ is applied to the latent state inputs fed to the actor, preventing unwanted gradients from flowing into the neural network's imagination pathway.

Furthermore, the reward function is smartly decomposed:
- Non-differentiable task rewards $r_t^{\mathrm{disc}}$ (such as discrete bonuses at the exact moment of passing a gate): Learned by a critic and optimized using value function gradients.
- Differentiable motion rewards $r_t^{\mathrm{diff}}$ (such as approach speed toward the gate or penalties for aggressive attitude changes): Backpropagated analytically and directly through the differentiable simulator's computational graph.

This design frees the world model from the burden of having to learn known quadrotor physics, allowing it to focus entirely on predicting external motion.

sections.heading: Outperforming Baselines in High-Speed Tracking and Dynamic-Gate Racing
sections.summary: DiffDreamer was evaluated on aggressive target tracking and dynamic-gate racing using the PyTorch-based differentiable simulator VisFly. It significantly outperformed existing RL and MPC methods in convergence speed, tracking accuracy, and gate completions.
sections.details:
### IV-A & IV-B Experimental Setup and Task Design
The experiments use the PyTorch-native differentiable simulator "VisFly." The policy uses an end-to-end design that directly outputs collective thrust and body rate (CTBR) commands.
- **Task 1: Aggressive Tracking**: Continuously track a target moving erratically and aggressively in 3D space, keeping it centered in a monocular camera's field of view at a designated desired distance.
- **Task 2: Dynamic-Gate Racing**: Pass through four dynamically moving gates consecutively in the shortest possible time.

### IV-C Learning Curve Comparisons
Baselines include DreamerV3 (pure world-model RL), BPTT (using only differentiable simulation), and PPO (representative model-free RL). As shown in Figure F5, DiffDreamer converged fastest and reached the highest rewards in both tasks. In gate racing in particular, while BPTT struggled due to a lack of external prediction and DreamerV3 suffered from physical inaccuracies and sparse rewards, DiffDreamer demonstrated outstanding learning performance.

### IV-D Performance Evaluation
Comparing external trajectory prediction accuracy (Figure F4 A, C), an Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) assuming a fixed model missed predictions significantly during sudden target accelerations, whereas DiffDreamer's world model predicted future trajectories very accurately, as shown by its scattered samples.

In quantitative evaluation of tracking (Table I), DiffDreamer achieved an average distance error of **$0.381\,\mathrm{m}$**—less than half that of Elastic Tracker ($0.793\,\mathrm{m}$), BPTT ($0.835\,\mathrm{m}$), and DreamerV3 ($1.003\,\mathrm{m}$). Looking at the target's position density in the body frame (Figure F4 B), DiffDreamer remained tightly concentrated at the center of the blue camera field of view.

In dynamic-gate racing (Figure F4 D, Table II), as gate speeds increased to $1.0, 1.5, 2.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$, MPC gate completions dropped sharply from 12 to 4 to 1. In contrast, DiffDreamer maintained **16, 12, and 8** completions, demonstrating superior robustness against fast environmental changes.

### IV-E Ablation Studies
- **Odometry and Relative Representation (Figure F6 Left, Center)**: Compared to reconstructing absolute target coordinates, conditioning on robot odometry with a relative representation led to significantly lower reconstruction errors and tighter tracking distributions.
- **Reward Decomposition (Figure F6 Right)**: Removing discrete rewards (gate passage bonuses) caused gate completions to collapse to 2, 2, 0. Removing differentiable motion rewards reduced them to 7, 4, 2. Peak performance (16, 12, 8) was achieved only when both pathways worked together.

### IV-F Real-World Verification
Using a custom 3.5-inch propeller quadrotor equipped with a Jetson Orin NX, identified physical parameters were reflected in the simulator, allowing the trained policy to run onboard inference at over 100 Hz. Using feedback from an external motion capture system, real-world flights successfully verified aggressive tracking and dynamic-gate passage matching the simulation results.

sections.heading: Summary: The Path Opened by Hybridizing Prediction and Differentiable Physics
sections.summary: DiffDreamer fuses a latent world model for external prediction with a differentiable simulation for self-dynamics, achieving outstanding convergence and control accuracy in agile drone control.
sections.details:
This study presented DiffDreamer, a novel framework for agile flight tasks that simultaneously demand external environment anticipation and precise physical control.

Decoupling the learning of the robot's own rigid-body dynamics from the world model and delegating it to a differentiable physics simulator significantly reduced the impact of model bias. Moreover, dual-pathway optimization—combining critic evaluation of non-differentiable task rewards with direct analytical gradient backpropagation of differentiable motion rewards via the simulator—enabled exceptionally smooth policy optimization even in hard-to-explore tasks.

This work represents a complete contribution, spanning rigorous evaluation in simulation, validation of individual components through ablations, and proof-of-concept real-world flight tests.

sections.heading: Future Challenges: Extension to Other Robots and Fully Onboard Perception
sections.summary: Current evaluations focus specifically on quadrotors. Applying the method to contact-rich systems like legged robots and validating noise robustness using only onboard cameras remain future work.
sections.details:
The authors frankly note the following limitations and future directions:

- **Target Robot Scope**: This study was evaluated solely on quadrotors, whose motion can be formulated relatively smoothly. Applying it to robots that involve non-differentiable discontinuous phenomena (contact dynamics), such as manipulator contact or legged foot-ground impacts, will require additional techniques.
- **Reliance on External Sensing**: In the real-world flight experiments, drone odometry and target/gate positions relied on an external motion capture system. Demonstrating end-to-end vision-based flight using fully onboard camera images for state estimation and moving-object detection, as well as evaluating robustness to real-world observation noise, remains future work.

takeaways: Assigning separate roles—delegating smooth, physics-known robot motion to a differentiable simulator and hard-to-predict external dynamics to a world model—is far more rational than mixing them into a single model.

Reward decomposition, where non-differentiable event rewards (gate completions, etc.) are estimated by a critic and smooth motion penalties are optimized via first-order simulator gradients, functions remarkably well.

Combining accurate system identification with a differentiable physics engine enables zero-shot sim-to-real transfer of high-frequency collective thrust and body rate (CTBR) policies to real hardware.
limitations: Because it relies on a differentiable simulator, its generalizability to discontinuous contact tasks—such as severe impacts or friction mode switches where gradients easily vanish or explode—remains unverified.
Real-world tests relied on precise pose feedback from an external motion capture system; noise robustness in fully onboard, vision-based flight has not yet been validated.
